content: If a mother living with HIV is on nevirapine, isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) should be initiated. However, regimens such as 3HR or 3HP should not be used alongside nevirapine prophylaxis. At the conclusion of tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT), a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) should be performed. If the test for TB infection is negative or unavailable, the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine should be administered unless the baby is living with HIV. If the test is positive, BCG vaccination is not required. Mothers taking TB medications can safely breastfeed, and it is recommended that the mother and baby remain together. The baby can also be breastfed while on TPT. Palliative care is a specialized approach aimed at preventing and alleviating suffering through early identification, accurate assessment, and treatment of pain and other physical, psychosocial, or spiritual challenges. It extends beyond addressing physical symptoms to include practical needs and bereavement counseling. Palliative care employs a team-based approach to support patients and caregivers, helping individuals live as actively as possible until the end of life. It is recognized as a fundamental human right under the right to health and should be delivered through personand family-centered care models integrated into health services. This care is essential for a wide range of diseases, including tuberculosis (TB). Palliative care for individuals with TB, particularly multidrug-resistant (MDR) or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB, has been underemphasized due to the focus on curative treatments. However, palliative care is critical for relieving suffering and should complement curative efforts. MDR/XDR-TB poses significant challenges, especially in lowand middle-income countries, with poorer treatment outcomes reported. Key symptoms requiring palliative care include breathlessness, pain, gastrointestinal dysfunction, night sweats, and hemoptysis. Formal palliative care should also be available when TB treatment is discontinued. For children and adolescents with TB, palliative care must address their unique needs. Drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) in children is associated with high morbidity and mortality, with common symptoms including pain, dyspnea, nausea, and vomiting. Social and spiritual pain may arise from stigma and isolation. Families often require support to care for the child and prepare for end-of-life care if the prognosis is poor. Integrating palliative care into existing services for children with life-threatening illnesses is essential to improve accessibility. The International Children’s Palliative Care Network emphasizes the need for pediatric palliative care integration into health policies, training, and equitable access to essential medicines, including opioids. Actions to improve access to palliative care for children include developing national policies, integrating palliative care into health systems, training healthcare workers, ensuring access to essential medicines, conducting research to demonstrate the impact of palliative care, and raising public awareness. Addressing respiratory symptoms in children with advanced TB or MDR-TB is particularly challenging due to limited evidence guiding management. Interventions such as nebulized saline, chest physiotherapy, and opioids (when necessary) may be used to manage symptoms like thick secretions or hemoptysis. They require adolescent-friendly services that minimize disruptions to education and provide psychosocial support. Adolescents are at risk of poor adherence to TB treatment, particularly during the continuation phase when symptoms improve. Factors such as family challenges, poverty, stigma, and treatment fatigue contribute to disengagement. Supportive relationships with family and healthcare providers can promote adherence. Adolescents also experience disruptions to education and future livelihoods due to TB and its treatment. Efforts to make TB services more adolescent-friendly include training healthcare providers in adolescent health, offering flexible clinic hours, integrating TB care with other health services, and addressing psychosocial and mental health needs. Collaboration with the education sector can help support adolescents with TB to remain engaged in school. Addressing basic needs, such as food security and financial support, is also critical. TB is a common cause or comorbidity in children with severe acute pneumonia, particularly in TB-endemic countries. Children with pneumonia who have prolonged symptoms, a history of TB contact, or treatment failure should be evaluated for TB. Bacteriological confirmation should be sought whenever feasible. Children with severe pneumonia and TB should be treated with a six-month regimen, as no data support shorter treatment durations in this group. Post-discharge follow-up provides an opportunity to identify and treat coexisting TB. The TB-Speed Pneumonia study assessed the impact of systematic molecular TB detection using the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay in children with severe pneumonia. While the intervention did not reduce mortality, it demonstrated the feasibility of using Ultra testing on nasopharyngeal aspirates and stool samples. The study supports the systematic use of Ultra testing in vulnerable pediatric populations.
